results.question: how long do i keep tax records
results.answer:
**How long you must keep business and personal tax records**

| Type of record | Minimum retention period | Why it matters |
|----------------|--------------------------|----------------|
| **General income‑tax records** (e.g., invoices, receipts, bank statements, and the supporting documents that back up each line of your return) | As long as the **statutes of limitations** for that tax year run out – usually **3 years** from the date you filed the return, unless a longer period applies (e.g., 6 years if you under‑reported income or made a fraudulent return) | The IRS needs to be able to verify or adjust any tax you filed.  If you can’t keep the documents, you risk penalties or missing a deduction. |
| **Employment tax records** (payroll, W‑2s, 941/944, FUTA, etc.) | **4 years** after the tax becomes due or is paid, whichever is later | Holds the employer’s side of the tax, in case the IRS wants to check wages, withholding, or unemployment tax. |
| **Asset records** (depreciation, cost basis, sale of property) | Until the limitations period for the year in which you **disposed of the property** ends (usually the same 3‑year rule, but depends on the transaction) | Needed to calculate depreciation, amortization, or gain/loss when you sell or otherwise dispose of the asset. |
| **Copies of filed tax returns** | Keep them indefinitely (or at least as long as the relevant limitations period) | They serve as a reference for future returns, amended returns, and in case of an audit. |
| **Other purposes (insurers, creditors, etc.)** | Don’t discard records until you confirm that no other organization requires them longer | If an insurance company or lender needs to see them for a claim or loan, you must keep them even after the IRS period ends. |

> “You must keep your records as long as they may be needed for the administration of any provision of the Internal Revenue Code … until the period of limitations for that return runs out.” [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=16)

> “If you have employees, you must keep all employment‑tax records for at least 4 years after the date the tax becomes due or is paid, whichever is later.” [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=16)

> “Keep records relating to property until the period of limitations expires for the year in which you dispose of the property in a taxable disposition.” [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=16)

> “When your records are no longer needed for tax purposes, do not discard them until you check to see if you have to keep them longer for other purposes.” [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=16)

**Practical takeaway**

1. **Start with the 3‑year rule** for most income‑tax documents (but watch for special 6‑year or “not limited” cases in the IRS tables).
2. **Add 4 years for employment records** if you’re a payroll‑paying business.
3. **Keep asset documents for the same period you’re keeping tax records for that asset** (usually end of the 3‑year period for the year you sell it).
4. **Never throw away copies of your returns**—they’re your permanent proof of what the IRS has on file.
5. **Check if insurance companies or creditors need anything longer** before discarding.

If any part of your situation is unusual (e.g., you’re selling a piece of property, have a large payroll, or have special deductions), you might need to keep documents longer than the basic period.  When in doubt, err on the side of keeping them a bit longer.



**Sources:**
1. [irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf (Page 16)](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=16)

results.question: why do i need to keep business records
results.answer:
You need to keep business records for several practical and legal reasons:

1. **Show you’re following tax law** – The IRS requires you to keep books that clearly show your income, deductions, and credits so you can prove you paid the right amount of tax. If you don’t keep the records that support the amounts on your return, you risk penalties and audits [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=12).  

2. **Support deductions and credits** – To deduct business expenses—whether wages, supplies, vehicle use, or start‑up costs—you must have the receipts, invoices, or other documents that prove those amounts and that they were ordinary and necessary [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=12)[[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=32).  

3. **Make tax filing easier** – Good records let you prepare accurate income statements, balance sheets, and tax returns quickly and confidently. Without them you may “forget” expenses or miss income that should be reported. [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=11)  

4. **Help manage and grow the business** – Records let you monitor sales trends, inventory, cash flow, and profitability, which are essential for making business decisions and securing financing [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=11).  

5. **Meet retention deadlines** – The IRS specifies how long you must keep records (generally until the period of limitation for the year on the return expires, e.g., three to six years, plus extra time for employment and asset records). Keeping records beyond that time can avoid inspection trouble if the IRS ever reviews a return [[4]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=16).  

6. **Provide evidence in an audit** – If the IRS examines a return, the records must be available to explain what you reported. A complete, organized set of records speeds up the audit and reduces the chance of disputes [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=11)[[4]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=16)[[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=32).  

7. **Prevent or reduce penalties** – If you can’t produce the required evidence, the IRS may impose a penalty of up to 50 % of the tax you failed to report, or the penalty for failure to file or pay on time [[4]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=16)[[5]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=41).  

In short, keeping thorough records protects you legally, makes tax compliance simpler, supports legitimate deductions, and gives you the data you need to run and grow the business effectively.

## Choosing an Accounting Method for Your Business When you first file an income‑tax return that includes a Schedule C (Form 1040) for your business, you pick the accounting method you will use for that year. After that, you must keep that method the same year‑to‑year, unless you get IRS approval to change it with Form 3115 or 1128 [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=14). Below is a simple decision guide that tells you which method is likely best for you, based on the information in the provided sections. | Question | What the IRS says | Recommendation (with notes) | |----------|------------------|-----------------------------| | **Do you carry inventory?** | If you buy​ or produce goods that you sell, you need to keep an inventory and use an accrual method for sales and purchases (unless you are a small business taxpayer that can treat inventories as non‑incidental supplies) [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=14). | **Yes →** Generally use **accrual**.

profitability [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=5). | Use accrual especially if you want accurate business, no inventory** → **Cash method** (easiest). - **Need precise matching of income/expenses, or you have a long‑term plan to add inventory** → **Accrual method**. 4. **Multiple businesses** – **Plan to change later** – Apply for approval with results.question: how do i check my workplace for hazards
results.answer:
**How to check your workplace for hazards**

1. **Start with a safety and health program**  
   • A clear program shows that safety is part of everyday work.  
   • It includes management leadership, worker participation, and a systematic way to find and fix hazards.  
   • Keep the program up‑to‑date and review it each year.  
   *[[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=5)[[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=7)[[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=9)*  

2. **Conduct routine self‑inspections**  
   • Knowledgeable workers should walk the shop, office, or store, looking for any condition that could cause injury or illness.  
   • Use the hand‑out checklists in the handbook – they cover general industry hazards, but you can add or delete items so they fit your own work.  
   • Record what you find, then decide how to control the hazard (engineering, administrative, or personal protective equipment).  
   *[[4]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=8)[[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=7)*  

3. **Keep records that help you spot problems**  
   • Combine the inspection list with injury/illness records, training logs, maintenance records, and any incident reports.  
   • Look for trends – the same type of fall, the same chemical spill, a sharp rise in slips, etc.  
   *[[4]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=8)*  

4. **Make safety a daily habit**  
   • Talk about safety with coworkers at the start or end of a shift.  
   • Ask workers to point out new hazards or ways to improve controls.  
   *[[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=9)*  

5. **Use the specific checklists for special areas**  
   • **Chemicals** – inventory, safety data sheets, labeling, PPE, eye‑wash stations.  
   • **Confined spaces** – permits, signs, atmosphere tests, lock‑out requirements.  
   • **Lock‑out/Tag‑out** – ensure machinery is de‑energized during service.  
   *[[5]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=38)[[6]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=40)[[7]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=66)[[8]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=50)*  

6. **Evaluate hazard controls**  
   • After you fix a hazard, keep checking that the control still works.  
   • If the problem re‑appears, adjust the control or add another layer.  
   *[[4]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=8)*  

7. **Use external help if needed**  
   • OSHA’s On‑Site Consultation Program offers free visits from trained consultants who can help you spot hidden hazards and suggest fixes.  
   *[[9]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=90)*  

---

**Quick step‑by‑step example**

1. **Schedule a weekly self‑inspection** (pick 3‑5 key areas).  
2. **Walk the area** and tick the items on a simple “hazard checklist” sheet.  
3. If you find a new wet floor, record it, then:
   -  Mark the area with a “Wet” sign.  
   -  If possible, place a non‑slip mat.  
4. **Later that week**, ask a coworker to look at the same spot; if it’s still wet, add a permanent drainage fix.  
5. **Update the program**: note the problem, the control added, and the date checked.  
6. **Repeat every month** to keep the workplace hazard‑free.

By turning inspections, records, and everyday conversations into a routine, you’ll spot hazards early, control them, and keep your workers safe.

results.question: cash or accrual accounting whats the difference
results.answer:
**Cash vs. Accrual Accounting – The Basics**

| Feature | Cash Method | Accrual Method |
|---------|-------------|----------------|
| **When income is recorded** | In the year you actually receive the money (or it becomes constructively available to you). | In the year you earn the money, even if you don’t receive payment until later. |
| **When expenses are recorded** | In the year you actually pay the money (or your liability is otherwise settled). | In the year you incur the expense – when the related goods or services are provided. |
| **Typical users** | Most sole proprietors and small businesses that don’t keep inventory. | Businesses that sell, produce, or buy inventory, or that need to match income with related expenses. |
| **Inventory rule** | If you keep inventory, you must usually use the accrual method for purchases and sales. | Same rule – inventory requires accrual‑based tracking of costs. |
| **Impact on taxes** | Easier to track cash flow; you report what arrives or goes out. | Allows “matching” of income and costs in the same year, which can smooth earnings and affect depreciation and inventory calculations. |

---

### How Income and Expenses Are Treated

- **Cash Method**  
  - *Income:* You add money to your books when you receive it. Example: you receive a check on January 4, 2025, after a job finished in December 2024. You report that check in 2025, not 2024 [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=14).  
  - *Expenses:* You subtract money from your books when you pay it. If you buy supplies in December 2025 but pay in January 2026, you claim the expense in 2026.  
  - *Construction*: The method is often chosen because it’s simple—it only tracks actual cash flow.  

- **Accrual Method**  
  - *Income:* You add income when you earn it (the “all‑events test” is satisfied). Example: you sell a computer on December 28, 2025, and bill the customer in January 2026; you still report that sale in 2025 because the economic performance happened that year [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=15).  
  - *Expenses:* You deduct (or capitalize) a cost when the liability is fixed and the amount can be determined. Example: buying office supplies in December 2025 and paying in January 2026 still lets you claim the expense in 2025 because the fact of liability is fixed in the first year [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=16).  

---

### When Inventory Forces Accrual

- If your business “produces, purchases, or sells merchandise,” the IRS requires you to maintain an inventory and use the accrual method for those transactions, unless you’re a small business taxpayer exempt from inventory rules [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=16).  

---

### Choosing and Changing Methods

- You pick your accounting method when you file your first business tax return. Once set, changing it normally needs IRS approval via Form 3115 [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=14).  
- You can mix methods in a **Combination Method**, but the combination must still "clearly show your income" and follow certain restrictions (e.g., if you use cash for income, you must use cash for expenses) [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=16)[[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=14).  

---

### Bottom Line

- **Cash** = “What goes in, what goes out.”  
- **Accrual** = “What you earned and what you owe, regardless of when cash changes hands.”  

The choice matters because it changes when income and costs hit the books, which can affect tax liability, perceived profitability, and inventory valuations. If your business keeps inventory or has long‑term contracts, the accrual method is usually required.

results.question: can i deduct business travel
results.answer:
**Can you deduct business travel?**  
Yes.  The IRS allows a taxpayer who is “doing business” to deduct ordinary and necessary expenses that are incurred while traveling away from home for that business.  The deduction is limited to the *business* portion of the travel and to the type of travel that the IRS recognizes.  Below is a quick guide to what can and cannot be taken off your return, with the specific IRS rules that apply.

---

### 1.  What counts as “business travel”

* **Travel away from home** – The trip must satisfy two conditions:  
  1. Your duties require you to be away from your normal “tax home” (the city or general area where you normally work) for a period **longer** than an ordinary day’s work; and  
  2. You need to get sleep or rest to meet the demands of your work while away.  
  – If either condition is not met, the expense is considered *commuting* and is not deductible.  
  – “Away from home” does NOT include the daily commute to your regular place of business.  
  – *Source*: [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=40)  

* **Places that qualify as a temporary workplace** – You can deduct the travel between your **home** (or primary place of business) and a temporary workplace that is either:
  * Inside the area of your tax home, or
  * Outside that area.  
  – *Source*: [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=35)  

---

### 2.  What can be deducted

| Expense | What you can deduct | How to calculate | Typical limits | Notes |
|---------|---------------------|------------------|-----------------|-------|
| **Transportation (air, train, bus, car)** | All ordinary and necessary costs for getting from home or a permanent office to the temporary work location **or** between the temporary location and another work site. | Use actual expenses or the standard mileage rate (2025: 70 ¢/mi; 2026: 72.5 ¢/mi).  If you pick the standard rate, you may also deduct business‑related parking, tolls, and any interest on a car loan. | *Standard mileage* 70 ¢ (2025) [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=35); actual expenses may include gas, oil, registration, etc. |
| **Taxi, limousine, commuter bus** | Fares between the airport/station and the hotel, or between the hotel and the work site. | Actual cost. | – |
| **Baggage & shipping** | Sending baggage, samples, or display material between home and a temporary workplace. | Actual cost. | – |
| **Car/truck driving (local and overnight)** | • If you use a car for business while **away from home** overnight, you may claim the business‑use portion of all operating expenses (actual or mileage).  • For local trips *within* your tax home, you can deduct the business portion of car travel but not the commuting miles. | See below. | *For local transportation, the business portion is based on mileage.* |
| **Meals** | • If the trip is overnight or long enough that you must rest, you may deduct the cost of meals.  • The deduction is generally **50 %** of the actual cost (or the standard meal allowance under Pub. 463). | 50 % of the meal expense, or the allowance. | *Limited to 50%* [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=41) |
| **Lodging** | Overnight or long‑duration stays required for the trip. | Actual cost, fully deductible. | – |
| **Cleaning** | Dry‑cleaning and laundry while on the trip. | Actual cost. | – |
| **Telephone & fax** | Business calls, fax, and other communication devices used while traveling. | Actual cost. | – |
| **Tips** | Tips given for any of the above services. | Actual cost. | – |

> **Reminder**: *All expenses must be separate from personal, living, or family expenses and must be ordinary and necessary for your business*【Segment 7】.

---

### 3.  How to split business and personal use of a car

| Method | Summary |
|--------|---------|
| **Actual expense method** | Deduct the business‑use percent of all deductible car costs (fuel, oil, repair, insurance, tolls, parking, etc.). The percent is based on the miles driven for business versus total miles. |
| **Standard mileage method** | Multiply the number of business miles by the IRS standard mileage rate. You can’t deduct other actual expenses that year, **except** business parking, tolls, and interest on a car loan. |
| **Choice** | You must decide once in the year you first use the car in business. In later years you can choose either method, or stay with standard if you are leasing the car. | *

results.question: what goes in an executive summary
results.answer:
An executive summary is the first thing most readers see, so it has to be short, clear, and informative.  
It usually consists of **one or two paragraphs** that give the reader a quick snapshot of the whole plan. In practice it should include:

| What to include | Why it matters | Source |
|-----------------|-----------------|--------|
| A brief description of the business idea or product/service | Sets the context and tells the reader what you’re selling | [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/320-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=4) |
| The amount of money you need and what it will be used for | Shows investors or lenders how much capital you’re seeking and why | [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/320-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=4) |
| How much money you already have invested or plan to contribute | Demonstrates ownership stake and commitment | [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/320-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=4) |
| A short schedule or timeline of key milestones or goals | Gives a sense of timing and progress | [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/320-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=4) |
| A quick note on the business’s strategy or competitive advantage (optional but helpful) | Highlights what makes your business unique | [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/320-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=4) |

Because it is a summary, you keep the language simple and avoid deep detail. Write it **after** the rest of the plan is finished so you can distill the most important points.  

If any of those elements are unclear or missing in your own plan, note which information you still need to gather so you can update the summary later.

results.question: how do i describe my target market
results.answer:
**How to describe your target market**

1. **Define the niche** – Start by saying who your “best customer” is.  
   *Choose a specific group of people (or businesses) that you want to serve.*  
   - For consumer businesses, you can segment by demographics such as age, gender, or income, by geography, by lifestyle choices, or by the benefits they seek from your product or service.  
   - For B2B businesses, you can describe the industry, company size, location, or how the product will be used.  
   *Example*: “Our target market is small, locally‑owned boutique coffee shops in the Midwest that want a single‑serve espresso machine with a built‑in grinder.” [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/320-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=14)

2. **Describe characteristics** – Give a few concrete traits that all members of the group share.  
   - These can be numbers (e.g., “annual sales $200,000–$500,000”) and traits (e.g., “values eco‑friendly packaging, prefers local suppliers”).  
   - The clearer the profile, the easier it is to design marketing messages.  
   *Example*: “They are between 25‑45 years old, live in urban areas, and spend at least $80 on coffee per month.” [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/320-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=14)

3. **Estimate size and growth** – Use data sources to tell how big the market is and whether it is growing.  
   - You can use population numbers, industry reports, or tax data.  
   - Estimate what portion of that market you can realistically capture.  
   *Example*: “The Midwest coffee‑shop market contains roughly 3,000 outlets, growing 5 % yearly; we aim to serve 2 % of them in the first three years.” [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/320-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=14)

4. **Tie it to value** – Briefly note why this group matters to your business.  
   - Explain the size of the opportunity and how your product or service meets their unique needs.  
   *Example*: “Because these shops need a compact machine that consumes less electricity, our product’s 30 % lower power use can reduce their monthly costs, giving us a competitive selling point.” [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/320-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=14)

5. **Review & refine** – Keep the target‑market description concise (1‑2 paragraphs).  
   - Update it whenever you learn new data or when market conditions change.  
   *Example*: After a competitor launches a similar product, you might narrow the target to “health‑conscious coffee shops that charge premium prices.” [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/320-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=14)

**Why this matters**

* A well‑defined target market lets you focus all other parts of the business plan—product development, pricing, promotion, and distribution—on the customers who are most likely to buy.  
* It also provides a concrete benchmark for measuring marketing success and for communicating with investors or lenders.  

In short, describe *who* you want to sell to, *what* they look like, *how many* there are, and *why* they need your product or service. That concise, data‑backed portrait is the foundation of a strong marketing plan. [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/320-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=14)



**Sources:**
1. [sba_business_planning_guide.pdf (Page 14)](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/320-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=14)

results.question: do i have to make my shop wheelchair accessible
results.answer:
**Short answer: Yes – if your shop is open to the public, you are required to make it wheelchair‑accessible, at least in the ways that are “readily achievable.”**  
[[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/316-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=6)

---

### Why a shop must be accessible  

* **Public accommodation** – Any private business that sells goods or services to the public (a shop, store, restaurant, etc.) falls under the ADA’s “public accommodations” category. That means the law applies to you.  
  [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/316-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=6)  

* **Objective of the ADA** – The purpose is to prevent people with disabilities from being excluded from everyday activities like shopping, eating, or using services.  
  [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/316-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=5)  

---

### What “readily achievable” means  

* The ADA doesn’t require a shop to be fully accessible if the changes would be extremely costly or difficult.  
* “Readily achievable” is judged by the size and resources of the business – a larger store is expected to do more than a tiny corner shop.  
* The rule allows you to start with the easiest changes (like widening a doorway or adding a ramp) and to add more over time as resources allow.  
  [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/316-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=6)  

---

### Core accessibility elements that are usually “readily achievable”

| Element | Typical requirement | How it applies to your shop |
|---------|---------------------|-----------------------------|
| **At least one accessible entrance** | A doorway that is 36 in wide and has no steps or a ramp with a 1:12 slope (maximum). Handrails if needed. | If you have more than one entrance, just one needs to meet this standard. If the other entrance is not available, you must provide a signed direction to the accessible one.  [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/316-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=10)[[4]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/316-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=11) |
| **Signage** | A sign that points to the accessible entrance. The sign must be legible and mounted within 48 in of the floor. | Needed if you have an inaccessible main door.  [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/316-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=10) |
| **Accessible parking** | At least one handicap‑designated space per 25 spaces (1‑26 spaces: 1 space; 27‑50: 2 spaces). The space must have a 5 ft wide access aisle and the international accessibility symbol. | If you offer customer parking.  [[5]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/316-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=8)[[6]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/316-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=9) |
| **Accessible sales/ service counters** | A counter that is no higher than 36 in and 36 in long with a 30 × 48 in clear floor space in front. | Needed at cash registers, ticket booths, etc.  [[7]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/316-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=15) |
| **Clear aisles** | A 36‑in wide route that is free of obstacles and has a 3‑ft turning space at corners. | Lets wheelchairs reach all merchandise.  [[8]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/316-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=14) |
| **Door hardware** | Lever or pull handles (not round knobs) that can be opened without gripping tightly. | Silly inconvenience but often easy to change.  [[9]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/316-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=12) |
| **Other “low‑hanging” barriers** | Replace steps with ramps, remove narrow turnstiles, add an accessible gate if a turnstile is mandatory, etc. | These changes are usually simple and “readily achievable.”  [[10]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/316-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=13) |

---

### If an immediate, full‑access entrance isn’t possible

The ADA allows you to provide **alternative service** while you work toward full accessibility:

* Offer home‑delivery, curbside pickup, or take‑out.  
* Provide a “service window” or lift if a ramp can’t be added.  
* Publicize the service so customers know they can order from outside the shop.  
  [[4]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/316-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=11)  

---

### How to get started

1. **Do a quick walk‑through.** Measure door widths, look for steps, identify parking spots, and note doors that are hard to open.  
2. **Prioritize the easiest fixes.** A simple ramp or a lever handle can often be installed for a few hundred dollars.  
3. **Ask for help.** The ADA Information Line (800‑514‑0301) or local technical assistance centers can advise on specific changes.  
   [[11]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/316-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=19)  
4. **Keep an eye on tax credits.** Small businesses may get up to 50 % of eligible accessibility costs (capped at $10,250) as a tax credit.  
   [[12]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/316-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=18)  

---

### Bottom line

Because your shop serves the public, the ADA requires you to remove “readily achievable” barriers to provide wheelchair access. Start with one accessible entrance, signage, and basic parking; add more over time. If you can’t make a full entrance immediately, provide alternative service options while you work on the changes.  

Feel free to reach out to the ADA Information Line or a local Accessibility Center if you need help figuring out the next steps.

results.question: am i exempt from injury recordkeeping
results.answer:
Whether you have to keep detailed OSHA injury‑and‑illness records depends on two things: the number of people you employ and the type of work you do.

**1. Small‑business size exemption**

If, during the entire last calendar year, you had **10 or fewer employees** (full‑time equivalents) you are *partially exempt* from the OSHA recordkeeping rules.  This exemption is set out in 29 CFR 1904.1 and the handbook states it here: “Employers are partially exempt from OSHA’s injury and illness recordkeeping requirements if 1) they had 10 or fewer workers during all of the last calendar year …” [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=14).

**2. Low‑hazard‑industry exemption**

A second exemption applies to certain *low‑hazard* industries.  OSHA lists those industries in 29 CFR Part 1904, Subpart B, Appendix A.  The handbook summarizes it: “…or 2) they are in certain low‑hazard industries.”  If your business falls in that list, you likewise do not have to keep the standard OSHA injury or illness logs.  (The same excerpt is in [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=14)).

**What you still must do**

Even if you qualify for one of the above exemptions, you **must still report**:

* **Fatalities** – any work‑related death must be reported to OSHA within 8 hours.  
* **In‑patient hospitalizations** – any worker admitted to a hospital because of a work injury or illness must be reported within 24 hours.  
* **Amputations** – any loss of a body part must be reported within 24 hours.  
* **Loss of an eye** – any loss of vision must be reported within 24 hours.  

These reporting requirements apply to all employers, regardless of size or industry, and are listed in the same section: “All employers, regardless of size or industry, must report work‑related fatalities, in‑patient hospitalizations, amputations, and loss of an eye to OSHA.” [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=14).

**Forms you would use if you are not exempt**

| Form | What it records | When it's filed |
|------|----------------|-----------------|
| **OSHA Form 300** (Log of Work‑Related Injuries and Illnesses) | Primary record of each injury or illness | kept on site for 5 years |
| **OSHA Form 301** (Injury and Illness Incident Report) | Supplemental details on each recordable case | kept on site for 5 years |
| **OSHA Form 300A** (Summary of Work‑Related Injuries and Illnesses) | Annual summary used for electronic submission | electronically submitted by March 2 of the following year if you have 250+ workers or 20–249 workers in a high‑hazard industry | [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=14)

If you are in the partial‑exemption category you do **not** need to keep the Form 300/301 log, nor must you submit the Form 300A summary, but you still keep the incident reports for any recorded fatalities, hospitalizations, amputations, or eye losses.  

---

### Bottom line
* **If you had ≤ 10 employees all year** or your business is listed as a low‑hazard industry, you are exempt from keeping OSHA’s detailed injury/illness logs and year‑end summary.  
* **In all cases** you must report fatalities, hospitalizations, amputations, and loss of an eye to OSHA within the specified timeframes.  

Check the OSHA “Low‑Hazard Industries” list (you can find it on OSHA’s website) to confirm whether your industry is exempt. If you’re unsure, contact your local OSHA Compliance Assistance Specialist, or call 1‑800‑321‑OSHA (6742).



**Sources:**
1. [osha_small_business_handbook.pdf (Page 14)](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=14)

results.question: how long do i keep injury records

• Worker medical and exposure records (e.g., hospital records, medical‑exposure documentation).
• Worker training records (e.g., first‑aid, safety training). | • Attachments to OSHA Form 300 and 301 must be kept **at the worksite for at least 5 years**.

results.question: what should i track for taxes and for travel expenses
results.answer:
Below is a short “check‑list” of the things you should keep track of for your tax return and for any business travel you take.  
Everything is taken directly from the IRS sources you provided, so you’ll see a citation after each item.

---

### 1.  Keep track of all business **income**  
* Any money you receive from customers, clients, or partners is taxable income unless it is excluded (e.g., certain sales‑tax receipts).  
[[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=2)  

### 2.  Record every **expense** that is ordinary and necessary for the trade or business  
* “Ordinary” = common in your field; “necessary” = helpful and appropriate.  
* Separate *personal* from *business* portions if the item is used for both.  
[[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=32)

#### a.  General business expenses  
Typical items you can deduct (or write off) on Schedule C (Form 1040) are:  
- Advertising, bank fees, licenses, legal & professional fees, insurance, supplies, repairs, etc.  
[[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=42)  
- Depreciation on property, including vehicles, equipment, and furniture (uses the §179 rules or the regular depreciation schedule).  
[[4]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=11)  
- Other expenses such as education, moving machinery, penalties, etc.  
[[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=42)

#### b.  **Home‑office** expenses  
* If a part of your home is used **exclusively, regularly, and for business**, you can deduct a proportion of mortgage interest, real‑estate taxes, utilities, insurance, and depreciation.  
[[5]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=41)  
* Use **Form 8829** (Expenses for Business Use of Your Home) or the simplified $5/sq ft method.  
[[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=42)  
* The deduction may be limited by your gross income from the business‑use portion.  
[[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=42)

#### c.  **Vehicle** expenses  
* **Actual expenses**: depreciation, lease payments, registration, repair, gas, oil, tires, insurance, parking, tolls, etc.  
[[4]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=11)  
* **Standard mileage rate** (70 ¢/mile in 2025) can be used instead of actual expenses; you can still deduct interest, parking, and tolls when you choose the mileage method.  
[[4]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=11)  
* Keep a **mileage log** if using either method; record date, purpose, starting/ending odometer readings, and total miles.  
[[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=2)  
* If you use a lease, choose the mileage rate for the entire lease period.  
[[4]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=11)

#### d.  **Capital items** – small‑item safe harbor  
If the cost of a tangible property is under the limit ($5,000 with a fiscal statement, $2,500 without) you can expense it in the year you buy it.  
[[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=42)

#### e.  **Other tax credits / deductions**  
* Consult Pub. 587 for home‑use, Pub. 463 for travel and meals, and Pub. 510 for excise taxes.  
[[5]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=41)[[6]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=40)[[7]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=8)

---

### 3.  Tracking for **travel expenses**  
When you travel **away from home** (more than a day and you need sleep/rest), the ordinary and necessary costs of that trip are deductible.

| Category | What to track | How to calculate |
|----------|---------------|------------------|
| **Transportation** (air, train, bus, car) | Receipts or logs of fares | Actual cost or mileage if driving (actual or standard mileage). |
| **Taxi / lim‑suite / commuter bus** | Fares between transit points (airport, hotel, work site) | Actual cost. |
| **Baggage & shipping** |Receipt for cargo, sample, or display material | Actual cost. |
| **Meals** | Receipts or per‑diem amounts | 50 % of actual meals (or 55 % for meals to physicians/foreign travelers); or use the standard allowance from Pub. 463. |
| **Lodging** | Hotel receipts | Actual cost. |
| **Cleaning** | Receipts for dry cleaning/laundry while traveling | Actual cost. |
| **Telephone/Internet** | Receipts for business calls | Actual cost. |
| **Tips** | Tipped amounts for above services | Actual amount. |
| **Business‑use split** | If using a vehicle or other expense for both personal and business purposes, document the business portion (e.g., mileage logs). | Divide cost by business miles ÷ total miles. |
| **Trip logs** | Date, destination(s), purpose, and business activities | File the log to substantiate the trip. |

*All of the above can be claimed on **Schedule C (Form 1040)** under “Business expenses” or “Travel expenses.”*  
[[5]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=41)  
[[6]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=40)  

---

### 4.  **Record‑keeping rules**  
* Keep a copy of every receipt, invoice, or bill that supports a deduction.  
* For travel, maintain a “trip log” with dates, purposes, and business outcomes.  
* For car use, keep a mileage log and keep receipts for operating costs.  
* For home‑office, keep a diagram or photo of the space and records of the proportion of the home used for business.  
* Preserve records for **at least three years** (six for certain tax‑preference items).  
[[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=2)  

---

results.question: do i need an ein and what accounting method comes with it
results.answer:
**Do you need an EIN?**  
- A sole‑prop or a partnership can use their individual Social Security number, but the IRS will issue an Employer Identification Number (EIN) automatically when you *apply* for one.  
- You *must* get an EIN if you:
  1. Pay wages to one or more employees, or  
  2. File pension or excise‑tax returns, or  
  3. Want a separate business‑tax ID that you can use instead of your SSN on returns and information forms.  

  If you have no employees and are not filing the special returns above, you can file as a sole proprietor with just your SSN. However, getting an EIN can still be useful for opening a business‑bank account, separating personal and business finances, or if you plan to add employees later. [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=4)

**What accounting method “comes with” an EIN?**  
- No accounting method is linked to an EIN.  
- The accounting method you pick—cash, accrual, or a combination—must be chosen when you file your *first* income‑tax return that contains a Schedule C (Form 1040) for the business.  You use the same method for income and expenses in that return and keep books that reflect that choice.  You can change the method later, but you’ll usually need IRS approval (e.g., by filing Form 3115).  [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=14)  

So:  
- **EIN:** optional for a solo proprietor without employees; required if you hire staff or file special tax returns.  
- **Accounting method:** chosen independently of the EIN, at the time you file your first Schedule C.  
If you are unsure which method fits your business, you can consult Pub. 538 or the IRS Interactive Tax Assistant.

**What injury‑recording forms do you need to keep?**  
- OSHA Form 300 – the *Log of Work‑Related Injuries and Illnesses*  
- OSHA Form 301 – the *Injury and Illness Incident Report* (a detailed follow‑up for each recordable case)  
- OSHA Form 300A – the *Summary of Work‑Related Injuries and Illnesses* that is filed annually with OSHA [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=14)

**How long must those records be retained?**  
- All OSHA injury and illness records—Forms 300, 301, and 300A—must be kept at the worksite for **at least five (5) years** [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=15)  

(If your business records work‑related infectious diseases, they must also be logged on Forms 300 and 301, and the same five‑year retention rule applies [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=48).)

So, keep the three OSHA forms and keep them on‑site for no less than five years.

results.question: what health insurance plan should i buy for my staff
results.answer:
**What health‑insurance plan to choose for your staff?** Below are the key points you need to keep in mind, drawn only from the handbook excerpts you gave. | What you’re looking for | Why it matters | How it shows up in the handbook | |--------------------------|----------------|---------------------------------| | **Group (collective) health insurance** – this is a “group‑hospitalization and medical insurance for employees” that most small businesses use. | • The premium you pay for it is a **deductible business expense**—it reduces your taxable income.
• It gives every employee the same coverage and keeps paperwork simple. | [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=37) | | **Add long‑term‑care coverage** (optional) | • This type of insurance is listed as deductible in the same spot as the group plan.
• It can be added to a single policy or bought as a separate rider, giving workers protection if they need long‑term care. | [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=37) | | **Keep it “qualified”** | • The handbook calls it “qualified employee benefit program.”
• In order to be deductible you must keep the plan’s paperwork and benefits in book. | [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=37) | | **Pick a plan that balances cost, coverage and flexibility** | • Think about what your workers need (hospital visits, prescriptions, specialist care).
• The hand‑out does not list specific plan types (HMO, PPO, etc.), so you’ll need to shop around—but the “group” letter in Segment 2 tells you that **any** group plan that meets the IRS definition of an employee benefit plan can be used. | [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=37) | ### Practical next steps 1. **Shop for a small‑business group health plan** with your insurer or through a small‑business group or trade association. 2. **Make sure the policy is named as a “group‑hospitalization and medical insurance for employees.”** That keeps it deductible. 3. **Ask whether the plan lets you buy an optional long‑term‑care rider.** 4. **Keep the plan rating and all the paperwork** because the handbook says you can deduct the premiums only if the plan is a “qualified employee benefit program.” 5. **Remember the deduction rules**—you can only take a deduction for the portion of the premium that actually benefits employees, not the entire premium if you sponsor only a limited benefit. **Bottom line:** For a small business, the simplest way to give your employees health coverage is to buy a *group health plan* that is listed under “group‑hospitalization and medical insurance for employees” (and optionally add a long‑term‑care rider). That plan’s premiums are tax‑deductible, fitting the handbook criteria on fringe benefits and insurance deductions. If you need more specific advice—e.g., whether an HMO or PPO fits your workforce or how to set up a cafeteria plan—you’ll need to consult a benefits broker or your tax advisor, because the handbook only tells you which type of plan is deductible, not how it should be structured. **Sources:** 1.
